title: Networking: URLSession, Codable & API Clients
scopeHtml: Scope: URLSession async/await, Codable, JSON decoding strategies, error mapping, auth/token refresh, uploads, caching, Retrofit comparison.

notes.title: Baseline and the networking stack
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Android you stack Retrofit (typed interfaces) on OkHttp (connections, interceptors, cache) with kotlinx.serialization or Moshi for JSON, all inside coroutines. In iOS the platform ships all three layers: URLSession (OkHttp), Codable (serialization), and async/await (coroutines). There is no Retrofit in the box; you write a thin typed client yourself.

Baseline for every note in this track. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum, SwiftUI-first with UIKit essentials. We use @Observable, NavigationStack, SwiftData, async/await, actors, Swift Testing (import Testing, @Test, #expect), async URLSession APIs and Swift Package Manager. Legacy forms (completion handlers, Combine, ObservableObject, XCTest) are shown only as "you will meet this in old codebases". Anything fast-moving is marked verify.

The layers.

  Your code        APIClient (protocol)  ->  Endpoint / Request builder
                          |
  Foundation       URLSession  (config, delegate, tasks, cache, cookies)
                          |
  CFNetwork / Network.framework  (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 QUIC, TLS)
                          |
  OS               nsurlsessiond daemon (background sessions), ATS policy

URLSession is a class, but its tasks run in the OS network stack. Background sessions are even executed by a separate system daemon (nsurlsessiond), so downloads continue while your process is suspended or killed.

Android iOS
OkHttpClient URLSession (+ URLSessionConfiguration)
Retrofit interface Hand-written protocol/struct; Moya or OpenAPI generators as options
Gson/Moshi/kotlinx.serialization Codable + JSONDecoder/JSONEncoder
Interceptor No chain; wrap the call or use URLProtocol / actor-based auth
Cache(dir, size) URLCache
WorkManager download Background URLSession
network_security_config.xml App Transport Security (Info.plist)

Real industry examples. Airbnb, Lyft and most large apps wrap URLSession behind their own client protocol; Alamofire (the best-known third-party library) is itself a wrapper over URLSession, not a separate stack. Apple's own Swift OpenAPI Generator produces typed clients over URLSession.

Everyday analogy. URLSession is the postal service with trucks and sorting centres; your APIClient is the mailroom clerk in your company who fills in forms, adds the right stamps and files the replies.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "iOS has no networking library, so everyone uses Alamofire". URLSession is complete; Alamofire is convenience.
  • Assuming a Retrofit-like annotation system exists. Swift has no annotation processors for this; macros and OpenAPI codegen fill the gap.
  • Forgetting the network stack runs outside your process for background sessions.

notes.title: URLSession async/await basics
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Android, a Retrofit suspend fun returns the decoded body, and OkHttp runs it on its dispatcher. In iOS, try await session.data(for: request) returns raw (Data, URLResponse); you check the status code and decode yourself.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
let (data, response) = try await URLSession.shared.data(for: request)
guard let http = response as? HTTPURLResponse else { throw APIError.invalidResponse }
guard (200..<300).contains(http.statusCode) else {
    throw APIError.http(status: http.statusCode, body: data)
}
let user = try JSONDecoder().decode(User.self, from: data)
interface Api { @GET("me") suspend fun me(): User }
// Retrofit throws HttpException for non-2xx and decodes the body for you
val user = api.me()

Key facts.

  • A non-2xx status is NOT an error to URLSession. Only transport failures (no network, timeout, TLS) throw. Retrofit throws HttpException for you; here you must check statusCode explicitly. This is the single most common bug of Android developers new to iOS.
  • data(for:) loads the whole body in memory. For big payloads use download(for:) (to a temp file) or bytes(for:) (streaming AsyncBytes).
  • URLSession.shared has default config, no custom delegate and shared cache/cookies. Create your own session for anything configurable.
  • Other async entry points: upload(for:from:), upload(for:fromFile:), download(from:), bytes(from:).

Streaming lines (server-sent events, NDJSON):

let (bytes, response) = try await session.bytes(for: request)
for try await line in bytes.lines {
    // each line arrives as the server flushes it
    handle(line)
}

Threading. The await suspends your task; the actual I/O runs on the system's network threads. It does NOT block the main thread, so calling from a @MainActor view model is fine. Decoding a large JSON on the main actor does block it, however; move heavy decode to a nonisolated async function (see the concurrency track J1).

Legacy form. session.dataTask(with:completionHandler:) plus .resume(). Forgetting .resume() is a classic old-codebase bug: the task is created suspended and nothing happens. Combine's dataTaskPublisher is the other legacy form.

Real examples. Apple sample code and the Swift on Server ecosystem (async-http-client on the server side) use the same async style. Many apps still contain a completion: based client wrapped with withCheckedThrowingContinuation during migration.

Everyday analogy. await is ordering a parcel and doing other things; the doorbell (resumption) rings only when the courier returns, and a "return to sender" slip (404) still counts as a delivery, so you must read the slip.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting data(for:) to throw on HTTP 404/500.
  • Forgetting .resume() on old dataTask code.
  • Loading a 500 MB file via data(for:) and getting a memory-warning kill.
  • Believing await on the main actor blocks the UI; only synchronous work does.

notes.title: Codable, CodingKeys and decoding strategies
notes.html:
Android equivalent. kotlinx.serialization uses @Serializable, @SerialName and a plugin that generates code; Gson uses reflection. Swift's Codable (= Encodable & Decodable) is synthesized by the compiler for structs and enums whose members are all Codable. No reflection and no annotation: the compiler writes init(from:) and encode(to:) for you.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct User: Codable, Sendable, Identifiable {
    let id: Int
    let fullName: String
    let avatarURL: URL?
    let createdAt: Date

    enum CodingKeys: String, CodingKey {
        case id
        case fullName = "full_name"
        case avatarURL = "avatar_url"
        case createdAt = "created_at"
    }
}
@Serializable
data class User(
    val id: Int,
    @SerialName("full_name") val fullName: String,
    @SerialName("avatar_url") val avatarUrl: String? = null,
    @SerialName("created_at") val createdAt: String,
)

Strategies instead of per-field keys. Set once on the decoder:

let decoder = JSONDecoder()
decoder.keyDecodingStrategy = .convertFromSnakeCase   // full_name -> fullName
decoder.dateDecodingStrategy = .iso8601                // "2024-05-01T10:00:00Z"
let encoder = JSONEncoder()
encoder.keyEncodingStrategy = .convertToSnakeCase
encoder.dateEncodingStrategy = .iso8601

Gotchas: .iso8601 does NOT accept fractional seconds ("...00.123Z"). Use .custom with ISO8601DateFormatter and formatOptions = [.withInternetDateTime, .withFractionalSeconds]. .convertFromSnakeCase maps avatar_url to avatarUrl, not avatarURL, so acronym properties need explicit CodingKeys (a famous trap). Other date strategies: .secondsSince1970, .millisecondsSince1970, .formatted(DateFormatter), .deferredToDate (default, a Double of seconds since 2001-01-01).

Optionals and defaults. A missing key for a non-optional property throws DecodingError.keyNotFound; a null for a non-optional throws valueNotFound; a wrong type throws typeMismatch. Optional properties (T?) decode as nil when key is missing or null. Unlike kotlinx.serialization, a property default value is NOT used by synthesized Codable: var count = 0 still throws if the key is absent unless it is Optional (the synthesized initializer ignores defaults). Write a custom init(from:) for defaults.

Custom decoding.

struct Price: Decodable {
    let amount: Decimal
    let currency: String

    init(from decoder: Decoder) throws {
        let c = try decoder.container(keyedBy: CodingKeys.self)
        currency = try c.decodeIfPresent(String.self, forKey: .currency) ?? "USD"
        // API sends "12.50" as a string
        let raw = try c.decode(String.self, forKey: .amount)
        guard let value = Decimal(string: raw) else {
            throw DecodingError.dataCorruptedError(
                forKey: .amount, in: c, debugDescription: "Bad decimal \(raw)")
        }
        amount = value
    }
    enum CodingKeys: String, CodingKey { case amount, currency }
}

Polymorphic payloads. An enum with associated values is Codable only if you write the container logic (Swift 5.5+ also synthesizes enums with associated values using a {"caseName": {...}} shape that rarely matches real APIs). The usual pattern: decode a type discriminator then decode the right payload, similar to a JsonContentPolymorphicSerializer.

Lossy arrays. One bad element fails the whole array. Wrap elements in a Lossy<T> struct whose init(from:) uses try?, a pattern used widely in feed apps so one malformed post does not blank the timeline.

Performance. JSONDecoder is reasonably fast but allocates heavily (Foundation JSONSerialization under the hood; Foundation was reimplemented in Swift in recent toolchains, verify exact speed claims). For very large payloads consider streaming, pagination or a binary format (protobuf via SwiftProtobuf). Never decode huge JSON on the main actor; Instruments' Time Profiler shows JSONDecoder.decode dominating hangs.

Real examples. Instagram-style feeds use lossy decoding; Stripe's iOS SDK has custom decoders for polymorphic payment methods; SwiftyJSON (legacy) and ObjectMapper predate Codable and appear in older code.

Everyday analogy. Codable is a customs form with fixed boxes; strategies are the translator at the border (snake_case to camelCase), while custom init(from:) is the officer who handles the odd package by hand.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting default property values to fill missing keys.
  • .convertFromSnakeCase and userID vs userId mismatch.
  • .iso8601 failing on fractional seconds.
  • Assuming one bad array element is skipped; it fails the entire decode.

notes.title: A typed API client with protocols
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Retrofit's annotated interface IS the client. In Swift you model each endpoint as a value, and a small client protocol executes it. The protocol makes it mockable, as you would fake a Retrofit interface in tests.

struct Endpoint<Response: Decodable & Sendable>: Sendable {
    var path: String
    var method: String = "GET"
    var query: [URLQueryItem] = []
    var body: Data? = nil
    var headers: [String: String] = [:]
}

protocol APIClient: Sendable {
    func send<R>(_ endpoint: Endpoint<R>) async throws -> R
}

enum API {
    static func user(id: Int) -> Endpoint<User> {
        .init(path: "/v1/users/\(id)")
    }
    static func updateName(_ name: String) throws -> Endpoint<User> {
        .init(path: "/v1/me", method: "PATCH",
              body: try JSONEncoder().encode(["name": name]),
              headers: ["Content-Type": "application/json"])
    }
}

The live implementation:

struct LiveAPIClient: APIClient {
    let baseURL: URL
    let session: URLSession
    let decoder: JSONDecoder

    func send<R>(_ endpoint: Endpoint<R>) async throws -> R {
        var comps = URLComponents(url: baseURL.appendingPathComponent(endpoint.path),
                                  resolvingAgainstBaseURL: false)!
        if !endpoint.query.isEmpty { comps.queryItems = endpoint.query }
        var req = URLRequest(url: comps.url!)
        req.httpMethod = endpoint.method
        req.httpBody = endpoint.body
        endpoint.headers.forEach { req.setValue($1, forHTTPHeaderField: $0) }

        let (data, resp) = try await session.data(for: req)
        guard let http = resp as? HTTPURLResponse else { throw APIError.invalidResponse }
        guard (200..<300).contains(http.statusCode) else {
            throw APIError.http(status: http.statusCode, body: data)
        }
        return try decoder.decode(R.self, from: data)
    }
}

Use from a view model with @Observable:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@MainActor @Observable
final class ProfileModel {
    private let api: APIClient
    var user: User?
    var error: String?
    init(api: APIClient) { self.api = api }

    func load(id: Int) async {
        do { user = try await api.send(API.user(id: id)) }
        catch { self.error = error.localizedDescription }
    }
}
@HiltViewModel
class ProfileViewModel @Inject constructor(private val api: Api) : ViewModel() {
    val user = MutableStateFlow<User?>(null)
    fun load(id: Int) = viewModelScope.launch {
        runCatching { api.user(id) }.onSuccess { user.value = it }
    }
}

In a SwiftUI view you call .task { await model.load(id: 1) }; the task is cancelled automatically when the view disappears.

Testing seam. A MockAPIClient: APIClient returning canned values replaces Mockito/MockK. A second seam is URLProtocol: register a custom subclass in a test URLSessionConfiguration.protocolClasses to intercept requests, the equivalent of OkHttp's MockWebServer. Testing detail lives in the testing track (see also J3 testing notes).

Alternatives. Moya wraps Alamofire with enum-based targets (similar to what we built). Apple's swift-openapi-generator creates client code from an OpenAPI spec (verify current package versions). GraphQL: Apollo iOS generates typed queries.

Real examples. Airbnb and Uber describe protocol-driven, codegen-heavy clients (Uber uses generated models from Thrift/protobuf schemas); Point-Free's swift-dependencies exposes the client as an injectable dependency with live/test values.

Everyday analogy. The Endpoint is an order slip, the client is the waiter, the mock client is a rehearsal waiter who always brings the same dish.

Common interview traps.

  • Making the client a singleton with global state, which blocks testing.
  • Forgetting Sendable on the client under Swift 6 and getting data-race diagnostics.
  • Building URLs by string concatenation (breaks on encoding); use URLComponents.
  • Not setting Content-Type for JSON bodies.

notes.title: Error mapping, retry with backoff and cancellation
notes.html:
Android equivalent. You catch IOException and HttpException and map them to a sealed Result. Same idea in Swift: a typed enum APIError: Error, and mapping of URLError codes.

enum APIError: Error, Equatable {
    case offline
    case timeout
    case cancelled
    case unauthorized
    case http(status: Int, body: Data)
    case decoding(String)
    case invalidResponse

    static func map(_ error: Error) -> APIError {
        if let api = error as? APIError { return api }
        if error is CancellationError { return .cancelled }
        if let url = error as? URLError {
            switch url.code {
            case .notConnectedToInternet, .networkConnectionLost: return .offline
            case .timedOut: return .timeout
            case .cancelled: return .cancelled
            default: break
            }
        }
        if let dec = error as? DecodingError { return .decoding(String(describing: dec)) }
        return .invalidResponse
    }
}

Note the two cancellation shapes: CancellationError (structured concurrency) and URLError(.cancelled) (the task itself). Treat both as "not an error to show the user".

Swift 6 offers typed throws (throws(APIError)) for closed error sets; its use in public APIs is still debated, verify team conventions before adopting.

Retry with exponential backoff and jitter. Retry only idempotent requests (GET, PUT, DELETE) and only for transient failures (timeouts, connection lost, 429, 502/503/504). Honour Retry-After.

func withRetry<T: Sendable>(
    maxAttempts: Int = 3,
    baseDelay: Duration = .milliseconds(500),
    _ op: @Sendable () async throws -> T
) async throws -> T {
    var attempt = 0
    while true {
        do { return try await op() }
        catch {
            attempt += 1
            let mapped = APIError.map(error)
            guard attempt < maxAttempts, isTransient(mapped) else { throw error }
            let backoff = baseDelay * Int(pow(2.0, Double(attempt - 1)))
            let jitter = Duration.milliseconds(Int.random(in: 0...250))
            try await Task.sleep(for: backoff + jitter)   // throws if cancelled
        }
    }
}

Task.sleep is cancellation-aware, so a cancelled caller stops the retry loop immediately, a property Thread.sleep lacks (never use it in async code; it blocks a cooperative thread and can starve the pool).

Cancellation. Cancelling the enclosing Task cancels the URLSession task: the await throws and the socket is cancelled. SwiftUI's .task cancels on disappear; .task(id:) cancels and restarts when the id changes, which is the idiomatic search-as-you-type pattern (add a try await Task.sleep debounce first). A task created with Task { } inside a view model is NOT cancelled automatically; store the handle and cancel it in the next call, as you would a Kotlin Job.

private var searchTask: Task<Void, Never>?
func search(_ q: String) {
    searchTask?.cancel()
    searchTask = Task {
        try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(300))
        guard !Task.isCancelled else { return }
        results = (try? await api.send(API.search(q))) ?? []
    }
}

Reachability. NWPathMonitor (Network framework) tells you the path status; use it to show a banner or defer retries, not as a pre-flight check before each request (the status can lie; try the request). Setting URLSessionConfiguration.waitsForConnectivity = true makes a request wait for a path instead of failing at once.

Real examples. Instagram and Twitter-style apps queue failed writes and replay them with backoff when reachability returns; Sentry and Firebase Crashlytics show NSURLErrorDomain -1009 (offline) and -1001 (timeout) as the most frequent network error codes in iOS dashboards.

Everyday analogy. Backoff is redialling a busy friend: wait a little longer each time, and add a random pause so thousands of people do not all call back on the same second.

Common interview traps.

  • Retrying non-idempotent POSTs and double-charging a user (use an idempotency key).
  • Showing an error alert when the user simply navigated away (cancellation).
  • Using Thread.sleep in async code.
  • Treating URLError.cancelled as a failure in analytics.

notes.title: Auth interceptors and token refresh with actors
notes.html:
Android equivalent. An OkHttp Interceptor adds the Authorization header and an Authenticator refreshes on 401, usually guarded by a Mutex or synchronized so only one refresh happens. URLSession has no interceptor chain. You add the header in your client (a few lines) and protect the refresh with an actor, which gives you the mutex semantic for free.

actor TokenStore {
    private var tokens: Tokens?
    private var refreshTask: Task<Tokens, Error>?

    func validTokens(refresh: @Sendable (String) async throws -> Tokens) async throws -> Tokens {
        if let t = tokens, !t.isExpired(skew: 30) { return t }
        return try await forceRefresh(refresh)
    }

    func forceRefresh(_ refresh: @Sendable @escaping (String) async throws -> Tokens) async throws -> Tokens {
        if let inFlight = refreshTask { return try await inFlight.value }   // join the running refresh
        guard let refreshToken = tokens?.refreshToken else { throw APIError.unauthorized }
        let task = Task { try await refresh(refreshToken) }
        refreshTask = task
        defer { refreshTask = nil }
        let new = try await task.value
        tokens = new          // also persist to Keychain (see persistence notes)
        return new
    }
}

Why a stored Task: an actor serializes access, but at every await the actor is released (reentrancy). Without remembering the in-flight task, ten parallel 401s would each start a refresh. Storing the task lets the other nine await the same result. This is the classic actor-reentrancy question in interviews.

Using it in the client:

func authorized<R>(_ endpoint: Endpoint<R>) async throws -> R {
    let t = try await store.validTokens(refresh: refreshCall)
    do {
        return try await send(endpoint, bearer: t.access)
    } catch APIError.http(status: 401, _) {
        let fresh = try await store.forceRefresh(refreshCall)   // refresh once, retry once
        return try await send(endpoint, bearer: fresh.access)
    }
}

Rules: retry once only; if the refresh itself returns 401/400, clear tokens and route to login (publish a sign-out event); refresh tokens are rotated by many backends, so persist the new one atomically before using it, otherwise a crash after rotation logs the user out.

Where tokens live. Keychain, never UserDefaults or plist (see the Keychain section of the persistence notes, 02_N2). No secrets in code; API keys that must not ship should be held by a backend proxy. Sign in with Apple, OAuth via ASWebAuthenticationSession, and passkeys are the modern login entry points.

Alternatives. Alamofire provides RequestInterceptor with adapt and retry methods, which is the closest thing to OkHttp's Authenticator; Moya has plugins (PluginType).

Real examples. Spotify and Uber-style apps use an auth layer that serializes refresh across concurrent calls; Firebase Auth hides this behind user.getIDToken().

Everyday analogy. Ten people reach a locked door with an expired key card. One goes to the desk for a new card while the other nine wait and then use the same new card, rather than ten people queueing at the desk.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing an actor prevents reentrancy; it only prevents simultaneous execution, state may change across await.
  • Refresh-storm: parallel 401s each trigger refresh.
  • Infinite 401 loops when the refresh endpoint itself needs auth.
  • Storing tokens in UserDefaults.

notes.title: URLSession configuration, caching and timeouts
notes.html:
Android equivalent. OkHttpClient.Builder().cache(...).connectTimeout(...). iOS: URLSessionConfiguration is a value you set BEFORE creating the session; it is copied and cannot be changed afterwards.

let config = URLSessionConfiguration.default
config.timeoutIntervalForRequest = 30        // idle time between bytes
config.timeoutIntervalForResource = 120      // total time for the whole transfer
config.waitsForConnectivity = true
config.httpMaximumConnectionsPerHost = 6
config.requestCachePolicy = .useProtocolCachePolicy
config.urlCache = URLCache(memoryCapacity: 20 * 1024 * 1024,
                           diskCapacity: 100 * 1024 * 1024)
config.httpAdditionalHeaders = ["Accept": "application/json"]
let session = URLSession(configuration: config)

Presets: .default (disk cache, cookies, credential store), .ephemeral (everything in memory, like private browsing, good for auth flows), .background(withIdentifier:). Default request timeout is 60 s, resource timeout 7 days (verify); a stuck request with default settings can hang a spinner for a minute, so set shorter values.

HTTP caching. URLCache implements standard HTTP semantics (Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified). With .useProtocolCachePolicy and a server that sends validators, a repeat GET sends If-None-Match and gets 304 Not Modified, which URLSession turns back into a 200 from the cache transparently. Other policies: .reloadIgnoringLocalCacheData, .returnCacheDataElseLoad, .returnCacheDataDontLoad (offline mode). POST responses are not cached by default.

Caching differences from OkHttp: OkHttp caches only if you install a Cache; URLCache.shared exists by default (small: about 512 KB memory, 10 MB disk, verify). Many apps forget to enlarge it and see no effective caching. For images use a dedicated library with decoded-image memory cache plus disk cache: Kingfisher, Nuke, or SwiftUI's AsyncImage (which has no built-in disk cache control and is usually replaced in production lists).

HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. URLSession negotiates HTTP/2 automatically through ALPN and may use HTTP/3 (QUIC) when the server advertises it via Alt-Svc (verify per OS version). You do nothing; connection reuse and multiplexing make httpMaximumConnectionsPerHost mostly irrelevant.

Metrics. Implement urlSession(_:task:didFinishCollecting:) to receive URLSessionTaskMetrics (DNS, connect, TLS, request, response timings). Production teams ship this to Datadog or Firebase Performance. Xcode's Network instrument and Instruments' HTTP Traffic show the same data. Charles Proxy or Proxyman work for debugging; they need the proxy's CA installed and trusted on the device.

Real examples. Spotify tunes caching heavily for audio chunks; most news apps (NYT, Reddit clients) enlarge URLCache and rely on ETags.

Everyday analogy. The cache is your fridge: ETag is calling the shop to ask "is the milk I have still the current batch?" instead of buying it again.

Common interview traps.

  • Changing the configuration after creating the session (no effect).
  • Confusing request timeout (idle) with resource timeout (total).
  • Assuming a default cache that is large enough.
  • Creating a new URLSession per request: leaks until invalidated, because a session strongly retains its delegate and defeats connection reuse. Call finishTasksAndInvalidate() if you must.

notes.title: Uploads, downloads and background sessions
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Large transfers that must survive process death use WorkManager with a foreground service or DownloadManager. In iOS the system itself runs the transfer: a background URLSession.

Foreground upload/download (async):

// Multipart or raw file upload
let (data, resp) = try await session.upload(for: request, fromFile: fileURL)

// Download to a temp file; move it before the closure/async scope ends
let (tmp, resp2) = try await session.download(for: request)
let dest = FileManager.default.urls(for: .applicationSupportDirectory, in: .userDomainMask)[0]
    .appendingPathComponent("report.pdf")
try? FileManager.default.removeItem(at: dest)
try FileManager.default.moveItem(at: tmp, to: dest)

Progress: the async APIs accept a delegate: parameter (URLSessionTaskDelegate) in which urlSession(_:didSendBodyData:...) reports bytes sent; Progress objects (task.progress) work with SwiftUI ProgressView(task.progress) via KVO. Always upload from a file or a stream (fromFile:), not from a big Data, to avoid holding it in memory.

Background sessions.

let config = URLSessionConfiguration.background(withIdentifier: "com.acme.app.uploads")
config.sessionSendsLaunchEvents = true
config.isDiscretionary = false          // true lets the system pick the best time (Wi-Fi, power)
let bgSession = URLSession(configuration: config, delegate: transferDelegate, delegateQueue: nil)
let task = bgSession.uploadTask(with: request, fromFile: fileURL)
task.resume()

Facts you must know:

  • Background sessions require a delegate; completion-handler and async data(for:) methods are not supported (only upload/download tasks via the delegate).
  • Transfers continue after the app is suspended or terminated by the system (not if the user force-quits from the app switcher; then the system cancels them, a frequent surprise).
  • When finished, the system relaunches the app in the background and calls application(_:handleEventsForBackgroundURLSession:completionHandler:) (SwiftUI: the .backgroundTask(.urlSession("id")) scene modifier, verify exact shape). You recreate the session with the SAME identifier, process delegate callbacks, then call the stored completion handler when urlSessionDidFinishEvents(forBackgroundURLSession:) fires. Skipping this makes the system penalize your app and kill it.
  • The downloaded file in didFinishDownloadingTo is deleted when the delegate method returns; move it synchronously.
  • Run time while launched is limited to roughly 30 seconds (verify).
  • Two sessions with the same identifier cause undefined behaviour; keep exactly one instance.

Resumable downloads. On failure, URLError.downloadTaskResumeData (via NSURLSessionDownloadTaskResumeData key) holds resume data; pass to downloadTask(withResumeData:). It works only if the server supports ranges and validators.

Real examples. Dropbox and Google Photos use background uploads for camera roll backup; Spotify and Netflix use background downloads for offline content (Netflix uses its own stack plus the system for assets; verify specifics). Podcast apps rely on .background sessions with isDiscretionary for auto-downloads.

Everyday analogy. A background session is handing a parcel to a courier company: you can leave the house (suspend or terminate the app) and they ring you when it is delivered, but if you personally cancel the order at the front desk (force quit) they stop.

Common interview traps.

  • Using async data(for:) on a background configuration (crashes or unsupported).
  • Not calling the completion handler from handleEventsForBackgroundURLSession.
  • Expecting uploads to survive a user swipe-kill.
  • Reading the downloaded temp file after the delegate method returned.

notes.title: App Transport Security and certificate pinning
notes.html:
Android equivalent. network_security_config.xml (cleartext rules, trust anchors, <pin-set>). iOS enforces App Transport Security (ATS) by default: HTTPS with TLS 1.2+ and forward secrecy ciphers for all URLSession traffic; plain HTTP is blocked.

Exceptions go in Info.plist under NSAppTransportSecurity:

<key>NSAppTransportSecurity</key>
<dict>
    <key>NSExceptionDomains</key>
    <dict>
        <key>legacy.example.com</key>
        <dict>
            <key>NSExceptionAllowsInsecureHTTPLoads</key><true/>
            <key>NSIncludesSubdomains</key><true/>
        </dict>
    </dict>
</dict>

NSAllowsArbitraryLoads = true disables ATS globally; App Review may ask you to justify it, and a blanket opt-out is a security-review red flag. Local network debugging uses NSAllowsLocalNetworking. Accessing the local network also needs NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription (iOS 14+), and failing to add it makes prompts or connections fail.

Certificate and public-key pinning. Pin to avoid a compromised CA or a proxy. Implement the server-trust challenge in a session delegate:

final class PinningDelegate: NSObject, URLSessionDelegate {
    private let pinnedKeyHashes: Set<String>   // base64 SHA-256 of SPKI, include a backup pin

    init(pins: Set<String>) { pinnedKeyHashes = pins }

    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession,
                    didReceive challenge: URLAuthenticationChallenge) async
        -> (URLSession.AuthChallengeDisposition, URLCredential?) {
        guard challenge.protectionSpace.authenticationMethod == NSURLAuthenticationMethodServerTrust,
              let trust = challenge.protectionSpace.serverTrust else {
            return (.performDefaultHandling, nil)
        }
        var error: CFError?
        guard SecTrustEvaluateWithError(trust, &error),
              matchesPin(trust) else {                // hash the SPKI of the chain certs
            return (.cancelAuthenticationChallenge, nil)
        }
        return (.useCredential, URLCredential(trust: trust))
    }
}

Always run the default trust evaluation first and pin ON TOP of it. Simpler, declarative option from iOS 14: NSPinnedDomains in Info.plist (pin by SPKI hash with NSPinnedLeafIdentities / NSPinnedCAIdentities) with no code (verify keys). Libraries: TrustKit, Alamofire's ServerTrustManager with PinnedCertificatesTrustEvaluator/PublicKeysTrustEvaluator.

Operational risk: pin the public key (survives certificate renewal if the key is reused), always ship a backup pin, and have a remote kill-switch/update path. A rotated certificate without a matching pin bricks the app's networking for everyone until the next release, a real incident type. Pinning does not stop a determined attacker with a jailbroken device and Frida/SSL Kill Switch.

Real examples. Banking apps (and apps like Signal, Revolut) pin; Facebook and Twitter historically pinned with remote-updatable policy. Many consumer apps skip pinning and rely on ATS plus Certificate Transparency (enforced by the OS).

Everyday analogy. ATS is "only admit visitors with a valid ID"; pinning is "only admit this specific person, even if the ID office would issue a valid ID to an impostor".

Common interview traps.

  • Setting NSAllowsArbitraryLoads to "make dev work" and shipping it.
  • Pinning the leaf certificate with no backup pin, then rotating certs.
  • Skipping default evaluation and trusting any cert whose hash matches in the wrong place.
  • Forgetting that a debug proxy will fail by design when pinning is on.

notes.title: Alamofire, Moya and when to choose them
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Retrofit adds ergonomics over OkHttp; Alamofire adds ergonomics over URLSession, and Moya adds an enum-based abstraction over Alamofire (like Retrofit over OkHttp).

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
// Alamofire (5.x): request, validate, decode
let user = try await AF.request("https://api.example.com/me",
                                headers: ["Authorization": "Bearer \(token)"])
    .validate(statusCode: 200..<300)
    .serializingDecodable(User.self)
    .value
// Retrofit
val user = api.me("Bearer $token")   // validation + decoding built in

What Alamofire gives you: validate() for status codes, request adapters/retriers (RequestInterceptor), ServerTrustManager for pinning, multipart upload helper, upload/download progress closures, Session event monitors, response caching helpers, cURL logging. Moya adds TargetType enums describing endpoints plus plugins and test stubs.

What you lose: a dependency to update (Alamofire ships major versions; watch Swift 6 concurrency adoption, verify), a larger surface to debug, and APIs that hide URLSession features. Since async/await in URLSession, the original pain points (callback pyramids, no validation) are mostly gone, so the pure-URLSession plus tiny client approach is increasingly the default for new apps.

Decision guide:

Situation Choice
New app, modest API URLSession + own typed client
Existing app already on Alamofire Keep it; wrap behind your APIClient protocol
Heavy interceptor/pinning/retry needs Alamofire (battle-tested adapters)
Large OpenAPI spec swift-openapi-generator with URLSession transport (verify)
GraphQL Apollo iOS
Real-time URLSessionWebSocketTask (built in) or Starscream (legacy)

Whatever you pick, hide it behind your own protocol so a swap touches one file; this also keeps view models free of third-party imports.

Real examples. Alamofire is in a large share of older Swift apps (the library's original author is the Alamofire Software Foundation, a spin-off from the AFNetworking family); Moya is common in apps from the 2016 to 2021 era; Kickstarter's open-source iOS app and many modern projects use thin URLSession wrappers.

Everyday analogy. URLSession is a professional kitchen; Alamofire is a pre-chopped meal kit. Fine, but you still need to know the knife work when the kit does not fit the recipe.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Alamofire is faster; it adds overhead, never speed.
  • Spreading AF.request calls through view models, causing a painful migration later.
  • Mixing up Moya (abstraction) and Alamofire (engine).
  • Thinking Alamofire works without URLSession; it is built on it.

notes.title: Production incidents, debugging and interview patterns
notes.html:
Incident patterns.

  • Silent decoding failure after a backend change. A server renamed a key; keyNotFound thrown; the screen shows nothing. Fix: log DecodingError with its codingPath, use lossy arrays, contract tests, and keep error analytics (Sentry breadcrumbs).
  • Refresh storm / logout loop. Parallel 401s each refresh, the backend rotates tokens, and later calls use an invalidated refresh token. Fix: single-flight refresh in an actor (above).
  • Main-thread hang from decoding. A 2 MB JSON decoded inside a @MainActor method freezes scrolling; MetricKit hang diagnostics point to JSONDecoder. Fix: decode off the main actor.
  • Retain cycle in a delegate. A custom URLSession(configuration:delegate:) strongly retains the delegate until invalidateAndCancel(); a view-model owning the session and delegate leaks. Fix: defer invalidation, or use URLSession.shared/one app-lifetime session.
  • App Review rejection / warning. Blanket ATS opt-out, or a missing NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription / privacy manifest reasons for required-reason APIs (from 2024, verify current rules).
  • Offline errors flagged as crashes. -1009 shown as fatal error banners; use friendly offline states and retry buttons.
  • Cellular surprise. Large downloads on cellular: set allowsCellularAccess / allowsConstrainedNetworkAccess (Low Data Mode, iOS 13+) and allowsExpensiveNetworkAccess.

Debugging toolbox. Xcode Network instrument; Proxyman or Charles with certificate installed; CFNETWORK_DIAGNOSTICS=3 environment variable for verbose logs; os.Logger for structured logs; nscurl --ats-diagnostics to test ATS compliance of a host; Network Link Conditioner (Additional Tools for Xcode) to simulate 3G, packet loss and 100% loss.

Rapid-fire facts for interviews.

  • Status codes do not throw; transport errors do.
  • Codable is compile-time generated; defaults are ignored; acronyms break snake-case conversion.
  • Task cancellation propagates to the URLSession task; check Task.isCancelled or use try Task.checkCancellation().
  • Actor = serialized access, not non-reentrancy; use a stored task for single-flight.
  • Background sessions: delegate-only, same identifier, call completion handler, killed by force quit.
  • Build the networking layer behind a protocol; test with a mock client or URLProtocol.

Real examples. Public post-mortems from large apps repeatedly show token refresh races and pinning rollouts as top self-inflicted networking outages; Cloudflare/Let's Encrypt chain changes have broken pinned or old-trust-store clients across the industry.

Everyday analogy. A production network layer is plumbing: nobody notices it when it works, and every leak shows up on the ceiling of a different room (a blank screen, a logout, a freeze).

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "how do you handle token refresh?" with only "interceptor"; the follow-up is concurrency of refresh.
  • Not distinguishing transport error from HTTP error from decoding error.
  • Forgetting idempotency when discussing retries.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• URLSession is the OkHttp equivalent and ships with the OS; Retrofit has no direct equivalent, so you write a small typed client around Endpoint values behind a protocol.
  • Async data(for:) throws only on transport errors; always check HTTPURLResponse.statusCode.
  • Codable is compile-time synthesized; use CodingKeys or key strategies, remember defaults are ignored, .iso8601 rejects fractional seconds, and one bad array element fails the whole array unless you decode lossy.
  • Map URLError, DecodingError, HTTP and cancellation into one APIError; retry only idempotent calls with exponential backoff plus jitter using Task.sleep.
  • Token refresh belongs in an actor that stores the in-flight Task to survive reentrancy; refresh once, retry once, persist tokens in the Keychain.
  • Configure timeouts and URLCache yourself; configuration is immutable after the session is created; avoid per-request sessions.
  • Background sessions are run by the OS, need a delegate, a stable identifier and the completion-handler dance; a force quit cancels them.
  • ATS enforces HTTPS; pin public keys on top of default evaluation with a backup pin and an escape hatch.
  • Alamofire and Moya are optional conveniences over URLSession; wrap whichever you use behind your own protocol.
  • Verify before relying on: exact default cache sizes, NSPinnedDomains keys, SwiftUI background URL session scene modifier, OpenAPI generator versions.
